rationale: B wins because it separates the real stories: P&L, driver cost/friction, and interoperability strategy. Its "Rivian adds Tesla-style plugs and opens its network with no automaker partner in sight" finds a real third lane, while A's "Rivian keeps owners cheaper as it opens the gates" is mostly a softer mirror of its outsider-premium angle. A is usable, but it makes the founder spend two bullets on the same pricing spread.
gaps_in_A: "Rivian charges rival-brand drivers more than its own" and "Rivian keeps owners cheaper" are the same price-gap fact with different protagonists stapled on. That is not real distinctness.
"retention lever the way it has for one walled competitor" imports an unsourced competitor analogy. Fine as a question with evidence; sloppy as framing from this fact block.
"Decay: week" on the owner-loyalty angle is generous. Without owner reaction, retention data, or a real price delta, that story cools with the announcement.
"They can place Rivian's move against the broader NACS-standardization shift" needs a current sourced peg or comparison. Otherwise it is a respectable topic wrapper, not a story engine.
gaps_in_B: "reclassifying a network it built for its own owners as a revenue stream" is a little too accounting-scented. Rivian says new revenue stream; reclassification is not in evidence.
"whether 'improves utilization' is a polite way of saying stalls sit empty" is a sharp reporter question, but it is still an inference. It needs a baseline before anyone pitches it hard.
"Did Rivian seek an automaker partnership and fail, or choose not to?" is useful but dangerous. Without an answer, it can invite speculation instead of tightening the story.
